title: Krishna's conch, Panchajanya
hook: Both armies blow their conches, and why Hindu worship opens with the same sound.
carry: the shankha sounds as worship begins
tomorrow: Arjuna finally speaks. where does he ask to stand?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Gita's first chapter gave Krishna many names, and we kept: each name of god opens a door. Before anyone speaks again, the field gets loud.
screen: `EACH NAME OPENS A DOOR.` → `THE FIELD GETS LOUD.`

segments.voice: In many Hindu homes, evening puja starts with a sound: someone lifts a white shell, takes a deep breath, and blows one long note. That's a shankha, a conch. Now the battlefield. The old grandsire Bhishma roars like a lion and blows his conch, and his whole side answers with conches and drums. Then Krishna lifts his own. Its name is Panchajanya, and it has a story of its own.
screen: `ONE LONG NOTE BEFORE PUJA.` → `CONCHES ON BOTH SIDES.` → `PANCHAJANYA.`

segments.voice: The Bhagavata Purana tells it. When Krishna finished his studies with his teacher, Sandipani, the teacher asked for one gift: his son, lost to the sea. Krishna went into the waters and defeated the demon Panchajana, who lived there in the form of a conch. The boy wasn't inside, so Krishna kept the shell, went on to Yama, the lord of death, and brought the boy home. The conch was named Panchajanya, for the demon it came from. So the shell Krishna blows at Kurukshetra was won by a student repaying his teacher. Here's the verse: panchajanyam hrishikesho devadattam dhananjayah. Hrishikesha blew Panchajanya; Dhananjaya, Arjuna, blew Devadatta. When the Kaurava side played, Sanjaya says only that the sound was a tumult. When the Pandava conches sound, he says the sound tore the hearts of Dhritarashtra's sons. Readers argue over that: is he leaning, hinting to the blind king how it ends, or just honest about what the sound did? Either way, the conch belongs to God. In images of Vishnu, one of his four hands holds a conch, and Krishna is honored as Vishnu on earth. Many families blow one before puja or aarti, and many say its sound announces that worship is beginning and calls the mind to attention; some say it clears away what's inauspicious. In many regions it sounds at weddings and festivals too. So when a conch sounds at an evening aarti, a family is borrowing one of the first sounds Krishna makes in the Gita: before a word is said, the house turns toward God.
screen: `A TEACHER'S LOST SON.` · `PANCHAJANYA: A GIFT REPAID.` · `IT TORE HEARTS. LEANING, OR HONEST?` · `VISHNU HOLDS A CONCH.` · then, large: `THE CONCH OPENS WORSHIP.`

segments.voice: Many Hindus sound a conch at the start of worship; here, let the breath be the conch. Breathe in fully, and let a long, slow out-breath carry a soft hum, like the first note of an aarti. If you pray, let that note be an invitation, the way a family's conch calls God and the whole house to attention. If you don't, simply listen to the silence after it until the next breath comes on its own.
Shankha: the conch. Krishna's is Panchajanya, won repaying a teacher; Vishnu holds one in his hand; and many homes still blow one as worship begins.
For the road: the shankha sounds as worship begins. Krishna's sounded at Kurukshetra; a family's sounds at evening aarti. See you tomorrow.
